Licence until the Nativity of St. Mary for Menaldus de Brocas and Michael de Fraunce to export from London to the city of Bayonne in a ship called la Seint Pierc of Bayonne, 400 quarters of wheat lor the support of the king's lieges there, on security given by Arnold de Garcy, Bernard de Bedoret, Ferrandus Myngouu of London, and William Otteford of the county of Bedford, that the same will be taken to the said city only. By C.

Protection, until Michaelmas for a great ship called la Seinte Marie 0 f Barcelona, freighted in the port of Bristol by tho king's merchants of the society of the Bardi with part of the wool granted to them by the king for great sums wherein he is bound to them, to take to their own parts and elsewhere, and for Francis Pedrosel, the master, and the mariners of the said ship. By C The same merchants have like letters of protection for a ship called lu Barfhelmeu of London, whereof Thomas Moneye is master, freighted in the port of London, to take wool to Flanders. By C.

Whereas Reymund Segnyn, the king's butler, Richard Chaucer, hia deputy in the port of London, and John de Wynnewyk, king's serjeantat-arms, lately appointed to arrest all ships arrested for the icing's 1342. Membrane 10—cont. passage which withdrew elsewhere, along with the bodies of the masters and mariners of the same^ pursuant to their commission arrested a ship oalled Gog Thomas, whereof John Boys of Dertemuth is master, in the said port of London; yet because Oliver de Ingham, seneschal of Gaseony, by letters patent shewn before the king and' council has testified that in his last passage from Brittany to Bordeaux the said John Boys convoyed him with the said ship for the security of the king's treasure then in his custody, the king has commanded the said Reymund and other commissioners, if the arrest were made on that account only, to- cause the same to be at once removed, and the ship with tho goods of John Boys to be delivered to him. cpr.text: Mandate to admirals, sheriffs, mayors, bailiffs of towns and ports a n ( j others not to arrest two ships, both called la Seinte Marie Gog of Dertemuth, whereof William de Asshendon and Walter Gentyl are masters, which were lately arrested in the port of London by the king's command because they came not to his last passage to Brittany, but are now released from arrest upon certain security in the chancery; provided that the ships be ready to go at the king's wages on the first passage of magnates and others coming to him beyond the seas. 1342. BerikhampDeo. 26. Berfchampstead. William son of Thomas de la Roche, staying in England, has letters nominating Gervase de Derby and Peter de Haulton as his attorneys in, Ireland for one year. The prior of Haverford received the attorneys by writ. By a petition of Gilbert de Umframvyll, earl of Anegos, it is shewn that there is a passage by the water called ' le Ee' of Kyme, passing through the lordship of his manor . of Kyme, between Dokdyk and Brentfen, as far as the water of Wytham on both sides, very convenient for ships and boats of those

Whereas the king lately appointed Thomas Crosse and Peter de Kennington. Gildesburgh to buy for his use the goods and merchandise of two ships called 'tarites,' taken from his enemies by Peter Bernardi de Tholosa, master of a ship called la Katerine of Bayonne, and his fellows upon the sea as prizes of war, and brought to the town of Southampton, and to deliver them to W rilliam de Kent, citizen and ropemaker of London whom he had deputed to receive and pay for the same, as in the letters patent is more fully contained, and afterwards the king commanded the mayor and bailiffs of the said town that, if the said Thomas and Peter should arrive within three days from the time of the arrival of the said Peter Bernardi, they should cause the goods or such of them as they wished to buy, to be sold to them at a price; and whereas although their attorneys arrived within the said three days the said Peter Bernard! and his fellows scheming to exclude the king from buying the goods, asserted that they had already Kennington. Kennington. Kennington.

Commission to Robert de Teye, William de Teye, Walter de Tilyngham and John de Norwico to make inquisition in the county of Essex touching a complaint of William de Cas that whereas he lately caused a ship called la distance of Dertemuth, whereof William W raryn was master, to be freighted at Bordeaux with wines and other goods and merchandise, to make his profit of in England and the ship while on its voyage was lost at the mouth of the Thames, although the said master and mariners and others in the ship escaped from the same alive whereby the wines and goods ought not to be called wreck of sea, men of the said county carried away much of this which had been washed ashore in divers places and unjustly withhold it from him, wherefore ho prays the king to order restitution of the same to be made to him ; and to certify him fully as to those who carried away the wines and goods, and into whose hands these came and the value of them, and whether the master and mariners of the ship escaped alive as is said. By C.

W 7hereas John Brocas, knight, John Elys, John Tuscanan, Bernard Guilliam of Bruges, Beymund de Casse, John de Mounbecon, Peter Arnald de Mauleon, Gerald de Lybourn, John de Mounbery and Arnold de Puche, merchants of Bordeaux, lately shipped in that city for London 304 tuns of wine, -in two ships called ' cogges ' of Flanders, and the wine was taken on the sea off the coast of Brittany, where the king then was with his army, by his ministers for his use and by his order was brought to Hennebon in Brittany and was afterwards stolen by his mariners, and whereas the king promised the merchants to pay the price of the wine amounting to 608/., to wit 40s. for each tun, when he came to England, but as yet they have had no payment, to their great damage; he grants that, as soon as William Casse and some other merchants of the duchy of Aquitaine, to whom he has granted the custom of 2s. due on every tun of wine brought to England by them and other merchants of the duchy, in the ports of London, Boston, Bristol, Sandwich, Southampton, Toppesham, Great Yarmouth and Kyngeston-upon-Hull, until t

Mandate to admirals and others appointed to arrest ships for the king's passage and all other ministers not to inflict or permit others to inflict any injury on John de Durango and John Boun, merchants of Spain, while lading in the port of London a ship called la Katerine de Castro of the portage of 160 tons, with corn which the king has granted that they may take to Spain, or in taking the same to that land hut to grant them safe conduct, during pleasure. By p.s.

Licence in like terms for John de Barando and Peter de Gray, merchants of Spam, for the passage of 440 quarters of wheat in a ship called la Seint Johan of Vermewe, whereof John Garcya de le Ketyen is master, arrested in the port of London by virtue of a like mandate to the mayor and sheriffs of London, on the mainprise of Peter Lopys and John de Notyngham of London. By C.

Whereas William Turk, citizen and merchant of London, is sending his ship called la Katerine of London, whereof William Chirchegate of Grenewich is master, laden with herrings and other victuals, with some of his servants to Bordeaux for the sustenance of some of the king's lieges there and to trade with otherwise for his profit as well as to buy wines there to bring to England, the king has taken into his protection and safe-conduct until Whitsunday the master and mariners of the said ship and the men and servants aforesaid. By C Windsor. Tower of London. Tower of London. Windsor.

Notification of the fact that whereas Arnold de Berueteres, citizen of Bordeaux, freighted a ship called la Plentee of la Hoke, whereof Edmund Aulak is master, for 500 quarters of wheat for Bordeaux and shipped the same in the port of London, the king's ministers afterwards caused the ship to be arrested for his service in France, the cargo to be discharged in the said port and the ship to go to him at Caleys, whereby the ship did not take the wheat to Bordeaux according to the contract.

ships: la Jonet of Hope of the Thames
cpr.text: Licence for William Heroun of London to ship 300 quarters of wheat in the port of London in a ship called la Jonet of Hope of the Thames, whereof John Gerard is master, and take the same to Bordeaux for the sustenance of the king's lieges there, he having found before the king in the chancery Henry Boresworth and John Wendovere of London as his mainpernors for the delivery of the wheat at Bordeaux in the presence of the constable of Bordeaux or such as supplies his place, and for the return of the ship to London by the quinzaine of Midsummer, if this be possible, with letters patent of the constable testifying that the wheat has been discharged at that city. By C. The like for the following, as specified below:— William de Stransale, Thomas de Santon, and William Bate; 300 quarters of any kind of corn, to be taken from the port of Kyngestonupon-HulI, in a ship called In Janus of Kyngeston-upon-Hull, whereof Peter Pygot is master. James Petyt, master of the ship called la Grace Dieu of Yarmouth ; 500 quarters of wheat from the port of London in the said ship for the sustenance of Bernard Ezii, lord of Labrit, and the men with him on the king's service in Gascony. Thomas Gysors and Henry Palmere of London, mainpernors. By C. William Gyn, master of the ship called la Michel of London; 500 quarters of wheat from the port of London in the said ship, for the sustenance of the said Bernard and his men. The same mainpernors. By C.

John Weryng, merchant; 300 quarters of wheat and 200 quarters of rye from the port of London, in a ship called la Grace Dieu of Houk. John Syward, citizen of London, mainpernor. By G. Richard Smelt, fishmonger of London; 400 quarters of wheat from the port of London in a ship called la Trinite of London, whereof Stephen Scarlet is master. Stephen de Brokesbourn and John de Pelham, mainpernors. By C. Arnold Berueters, merchant of Bordeaux; 500 quarters of wheat from the same port in a ship called la Leonard of Colecestre, whereof John Lucas is master. Ralph Beauflour and John Finch of London, mainpernors. By C.

Licence for John Siward of London to take to Bordeaux 350 quarters of wheat from the port of London in a ship called la Cogge Johan of Chalke, whereof Bichard Frende is master, provided that that ship be not of the number of those hundred and fifty ships ordered to go to sea on the king's service and the going of those ships be not hindered by this licence. The said John has found before the king in the chancery Henry Fannere and Henry Palmere of London as mainpernors that the wheat will be taken to Bordeaux and nowhere else and that the ship will return if possible by St. Peter's Chains with letters patent of the constable of Bordeaux attesting the discharge of the wheat there. By p.s. The like for the following :— John de Wesenham, the king's butler, and Thomas de Biteryng; 300 quarters of divers kinds of corn from the port of Lynn in a ship called la Nicholas of Lynn, whereof William Bleye is master. Geoffrey Drewe and Alexander de Lonewade, mainpernors. By C.

Licence for Reyniund son of Reymund Seguyn, in consideration of the manifold services of his father, the late chief butler, and because he has freely delivered for the king's use 20 tuns of his own wine lately bought in the duchy of Aquitaine, to be paid for in the wardrobe, and is to go immediately, as he asserts, to the same duchy to buy more wine for the sustenance of the king and his lieges to bring to England, to take to Bordeaux from the port of London in a ship called la Cogye Thomas of Dertemuth, whereof Thomas Swet is master, 150 quarters of wheat, 50 quarters of beans, 50 quarters of rye, and 50 quarters of peas, for the sustenance of the king's lieges there; he having found before the king in the chancery Gaillard Sedatz, citizen of London, and William de Lynyac of Bordeaux as mainpernors for his taking the corn to Bordeaux and nowhere else, and the return of the ship with all speed bringing letters patent of the constable of Bordeaux testifying to the due delivery of the same there. By C.

By C.

cpr.text: Protection, until Michaelmas, for Henry Byle, master of a ship called la Katerine of Sandwich, charged by the king to carry to London by sea the stone and other things necessary for his chapel in Westminster Palace ; and for the ship with the mariners therein. Tower of London.

Protection, until Christmas, - for Richard Smelt and Thomas Blod, citizens of London, who are sending two little ships called ' vytaillers,' one called la Nicholas of London and the other la Anne of London, whereof Geoffrey Fyssher and Adam Kanne of Grenewych are masters, to bring salt salmon from Berwick-on-Tweed to London, and for the ships with the goods of the said Richard and Thomas already shipped therein and to be shipped therein. By C.

Protection, and safe conduct, until Michaelmas, for William son of William le Palmere of Normandy, lately impeached of divers plunderings and trespasses committed on merchants of London at sea and on that account arrested and detained under arrest in the said city, who is innocent of the said trespasses as has been found by a trial thereof made at Brugges in Flanders by the king's command and returned into the chancery, and is now going to his own parts. 1352. Westminster Membrane 12—cont. The like, for one year, for Wikemann Nannessone, master of a ship called la Godeship, and Helmuth Vandermagne, master of a ship called Skyntwyne of Seland, coming to England with their ships and merchan­ dise. By C.

Protection and safe-conduct, during pleasure, pursuant to the treaty between the king and his subjects and the duke of Genoa and his subjects and the whole commonalty of Genoa, for Anthony de Compaignon, merchant of the said parts of Genoa, master of a ship called The Blessed Mary Crowned, who lately came to London with the said ship laden with avoirdupois and is going to his own or other parts for other merchandise to bring to England; and for his men, mariners and servants in the ship. By C.

B y K. on the information of John de Bello Campo.

Appointment of John de Haddon, king's serjeant at arms, to take i n the counties of York and Lincoln forty mariners and put them on the king's ship called la Charite in the port of Kyngeston upon Hull to bring the ship to London, committing to prison all mariners found rebellious herein. By K.

Protection, during pleasure, for Gerard Goldyng, master of a ship called la Thomas of the portage of 20 tuns of wine and no more, wherein Thomas, bishop of Durham, who stays on the safe-guard of the marches towards Scotland, has shipped in the port of London, victuals purveyed in the said city for the expenses of his household to be brought to him to Norham, and for four mariners and two grooms serving in the ship, in taking the victuals from London to Bamburgh. By C.

Writ of aid, for one year, for Daniel de Rouclif and William Cok, servants of John, archbishop of York, the chancellor, appointed by him to purvey corn and other victuals in the county of Lincoln and have them brought to London in a ship called la Nicolas of Barton for the expenses of the household of the chancery. March 26.

Commission to Adam de Acres and Robert de Naylynghirst to make inquisition in the counties of Essex and Suffolk touching a complaint by Henry Pycard, the king's butler, containing that he had caused a number of tuns of wine to be bought for the king in Gascony and loaded there in a ship called la James of Fobbynge for London, that the ship was accidentally broken in the mouth of the water of Thames near Recolvre, the master and mariners therein coming safely to land, and that great quantity of the wine came to places in the said counties and was taken by men of the same, and although he appointed Thomas atte Stone, his lieutenant in the port of Ipswich, to search for such wines, signed with the sign of the said butler, and Thomas came to the house of Richard Cock of Maldon and other places where some of the wines, as he was informed, were lodged to make search for and take the same into the king's hands, the said Richard and others contemptuously resisted him not per­ mitting him to make search or survey the wines ; to find where the wines are and bring them into the king's hands, ar

Licence for Richard Haverlond of Ipswich, in consideration of the loss of his ship called la Nicholas, laden at Bordeaux with wines for London, at sea in the entry of the port of Sandwich, to take 100 quarters of wheat as above. Feb. 12.

Licence for Nicholas de Brokworth and Andrew Pikeman of London to buy 200 quarters of corn and other victuals and merchandise in the counties of York and Northumberland and bring the same to London in a ship called la Nicholas of London, as John le Rous and Robert de Rameseye of London have mainprised in the chancery that he will bring the same to London and nowhere else, and protection for them and their men and servants in buying the corn & c , and for the master and mariners of the ship in bringing the same to London; until Midsummer.

Whereas a ship called la Bodecogg of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, whereof Nicholas de Wylyngton is master, was arrested in Flanders by John Malewayn to come to the fleet of the king's ships in England ordained for the defence of the realm, because of that arrest came to the port of London before the fleet assembled there left the port and was ready to go in the fleet, but, as some of the mariners of the same were taken for the manning of other ships of the fleet, the said ship after the progress of the fleet from the port was left behind empty, and whereas the said master has made oath before the king that he and the ship will be ready for the king's service when he shall summon him, the king has granted licence for the master to go to his own parts or elsewhere as shall be most to his advantage, during the king's pleasure.

Commission to Stephen de Cavendyssh, mayor of London, Roger Roter, mayor of the staple of , John Lovekyn, Adam Fraunceys and TUard de Usflet, to make inquisition in the city of London in the presence of William de Hoi beech, late one of the sheriffs of the city, touching a petition of Peter de Grymesby shewn before the king in the present Parliament, setting forth that, whereas he freighted a ship of his called la George to certain merchants to bring wools and other merchandise to Flanders and they laded the ship in the port of Kyngeston upon Hull with wools and other merchandise for those parts, paying the customs and subsidies due, because some of the mariners of the ship without the knowledge of petitioner and of the master of the ship hid wools and wool-fells in their beds and chests in the ship and brought these to Flanders without payment of the customs due, the ship has been arrested in the port of London by the said William as forfeit to the king, and praying that the king, taking into consideration that he and the master were blameless in regard to the trespass an

The like for Martin Ocheo, master of a ship called la Seint James of Castro in Spain and his fellows, the mariners of the said ship, to buy with 50/. of 256 marks for which they have sold 32 tuns of wine brought to London by them from Spain, woollen cloths to take to Spain with them. Nov. 20.

Licence, until Michaelmas, for John de Pleseys, merchant of Garraunde in Brittany, of the obedience of John, duke of Brittany, who freighted two little crayers, one called la Stint Michel and the other la Touz Seintz, of Garraunde and of Bares, in the port of Garraunde with salt to the value of 120/., brought the same to London and sold it there, to buy in England cloths and other wares to that value, ship these in the crayers in the port of London and take them to Garraunde to make his profit of them. By C.

Pardon to William Janekin, master of a ship called la Seinte Mariebote of London, of the king's suit for the death of Richard Ricard of Chalk, and of any consequent outlawry ; as the king is informed that he killed him in self defence. By p.s.

Pardon to John de Raus, master of a ship called le Seintespirit of Bayon, and the mariners of the ship, of their trespass and the forfeiture incurred by them in crossing by night from the port of London against the usual custom with the ship, and with 40 ells of uncustomed cloth in divers parcels, and 31/. and 40c/. in gold and certain other things enclosed in a sack, which were arrested for that reason; and mandate to all admirals &c. not to interfere with the ship, which has been released. By K.

Commission to Peter de Brugge, sheriff of Southampton, and the king's Serjeants at arms Richard de Imworth and John de Basyng, reciting that, because the king is given to understand that a ship of Brittany laden with divers goods and wares was taken at sea by some of the king's mariners, that he afterwards, in consideration of his son the duke of Brittany, delivered the ship to those from whom it was taken, with the goods and wares, to make their profit of the same, and granted safe conduct and protection for the ship, and the merchants and the mariners of the same, who in reliance on the safe conduct and protection sailed to the port of Hamelhoke. and anchored there, and that there some evildoers in a ship called la Michel of Hull committed atrocious assaults on the merchants and mariners, killed John son of John atte Wode of London, merchant, and many others, and robbed the said John of 200 marks in money by tale, and the others of goods and merchandise, he has appointed them to make inquisition by the oath of good men of the county of Southampton touching the premises

Safe conduct and protection, for one year, for John de Proll, merchant of La Grune in Portugal, who lately brought to London in his ship called le Seint Thomas from the port of Lucebon wines of Henry Herbury and William Baret, merchants of London, and for his said ship, the mariners thereof and all goods and things therein; as the said Henry and William have testified before the king in the Chancery that he is of the land and dominion of the king of Portugal and of the king's friendship, as the other subjects of that king are, and that he discharged the wines in London. Jan. 20.

Commission to William de Appuldrefeld, John Haddon, Peter Rede, Thomas Elys, Arnold Broun and William Benet,—on petition made on behalf of William Canynges, John Stodeye, Nicholas Brambre and other citizens of London, that whereas they caused a ship called le Nicholas of Bayonne, whereof Stephen de Carreys was master, to be loaded at Bayonne in Gascony with wines and iron for London, and the said ship was imperilled and broken at Godewynsonde, co. Kent, the goods thrown ashore and saved and the mariners landed in safety, divers men of the said county have occupied and detained the goods,—to make inquisition in the said county touching the premises and restore to the merchants the goods which they can prove by their signs or otherwise to be theirs, in case it be found by the inquisition that they ought not to pertain to the king or other lords of liberties as wreck. without the king's licence. By C.

Commission to William Filel, John Elmerigge, Alexander de Rixton, clerk, Robert Manyford and William Shike,—on petition made on behalf of John de Stodeye, William de Tongge, Nicholas Brambre and Thomas Gysors, merchants of London, and Robert de Knolles, ' chivaler,' shewing that, whereas they loaded a ship called la Welfare of Dertmuth, whereof William Colyn is master, at Plymmuth with 50 tuns of wine, 20 thousand of iron and tin, 10 thousand of ' hake,' and divers other wares, as well as very many goods, jewels and harness of the said Robert, to wit, wallets, great and small, halls and chambers of linen cloth and silk, robes, vestures and other jewels, and silver vessels in casks for London, and the said ship was broken at Warham, co. Dorset, the goods therein cast ashore and salved, and the mariners came safe to land, nevertheless the wines, merchandise, goods, jewels and harness are occupied and detained by men of that county,—to make inquisition in the county touching the premises and restore to the merchants and Robert any goods they can prove to be theirs, in case it be found b

Safe conduct and protection, until Midsummer, for Henry Bettesson of Durdraght, master of a ship called la Katerine of Durdraght, laden with cloths and other merchandise of merchants of London and Florence, and the mariners of the said ship, in going from the port of London to Burdeux or Lucebon, and returning to London. And be it remembered that John Pyel, citizen of London, has mainperned in the Chancery that the said ship and merchandise shall not pass the coast of Sandwich called ' les Dounes ' without other mandate of the king, or at least until the king has left the coasts of England with his fleet. The like letters for James Bettesson of Durdraght, master of a ship called la Sainte Marie Knaught of Durdraght, going as above. And be it remembered that John Pyel has mainperned as above.

Whereas the mayor and aldermen of London have certified the king under the mayor's seal that William de Neuport, citizen and 1373 Membrane 8—cont. fishmonger of London, lately laded at the town of Yarum in Tese a ship called la Aungel of Flecchyng in Seland, whereof Peter Fek of Flecchyng in Seland is lord and master, with 300 quarters of wheat, worth 1201., to be brought to Queenhithe in the port of London to be discharged there, and on the voyage the said Peter, of his own will, maliciously struck another ship belonging to Giles Person of Seland laden with 240 quarters of wheat whereof 120 quarters belonged to the said William de Neuport and the remaining 120 quarters to William de Bury, fishmonger, and others, whereby the ship of Giles Person was broken and the wheat in it, by default of Peter, totally lost, as was found before the mayor and bailiffs of Newcastle-upon-Tyne at the suit of the attorney of William de Bury, and upon this Peter found security to satisfy William de Bury for his part of the wheat, but immediately after took his course to Zeland with his ship

Commission to John Botild of Lowystoft, Robert Rust of Blakeney and Geoffrey Sterlyng of Ipswich to arrest and bring honourably before the king and council William Baker, master of the barge of Yarmouth, and John Covenant, merchant of the water of Humbre ; on complaint by John Burgeys of Quenesburgh, one of the king's mariners, and John Blakeney, citizen and merchant of London, that while their ship called la Marie of Fobbyng, laden with their goods and merchandise for Bordeaux, was lying anchored at Brest in Brittany among other ships of English merchants, the said William and. John ran into their said ship with the said barge and maliciously cut the ropes wherewith it was anchored, so that it was driven on to the sands and sea coast of Brittany and all their goods were lost.

The like to Guy de Brian, Robert Bealknap, Robert Fitz Payn, Hugh Tyrel, Henry de Percehay, William de Lucy and Walter de Clopton, on complaint by Robert Knolles that, whereas he freighted a ship called la Welfare of Dertmuth in the port of Plymmouthe with goods for London, and on the voyage the ship was driven by the violence of the sea to Kymerych in Purbik, co. May 4.

Grant to John Mountagu of the city of Salisbury, in consideration of his good service and losses in the king's service, of a ship called la Kaiherine de la Tour lying in the river Thames, much broken, with all its gear. By p.s.

Commission to John Michell, Robert Markeley and Richard Kays, Maidstone. Serjeants at arms, on complaint by Richard Garner of Pymond and other merchants of Genoa dwelling in the city of London, that whereas they caused a ship called la Marie Kntjijht of Leselus in Flanders, of which Arnald Conyng is master, to be freighted at La Rochelle with wine of La Rochelle and other merchandise to take to London for sale, the said ship with the wines and merchandise when sailing at sea towards the said city was captured by certain of the king's lieges of the town of Dertemouth and other adjoining towns, contrary to the form of the treaty between the king and those of Flanders and the king's letters of safe-conduct to them, to enquire into the matter and cause restitution to be made or, in default, to compel the owners, masters and victuallers of the ships, barges and balingers to find security for their appearance in person before the king and council in Chancery in the quinzaine of Easter next or, if they refuse, to arrest them and bring them there.

Commission to William Maryot and Robert Crowemer to enquire into the petition of Walter Cherteseye, John Femell, Simon Seman, Robert Hierne, Ralph Valentyn, John Melbourne and John Treweman of London, merchants, that whereas they lately freighted a ship called le Petyr of Dertemouth at the city of Bordeaux with certain wines to come to London and it was broken by tempest on its passage at the entrance of the river Thames and the persons in it were divinely saved and all the wines came afterwards to divers coasts of the realm, viz. to the counties of Norfolk, Suffolk and Lincoln, and are still in the hands of divers lieges of the king, restitution may be made to them. March 20.

April 3.

Commission to John Bekwyth, master of a ship called le Bernard of London, to take 40 mariners to serve the king in the said ship for the taking of the duke of Burbon, the king's prisoner, from England to the town of Diepe in the duchy of Normandy. By C.
Commission to Thomas Martyn, master of a ship called le Gabriel 'of London, to take sixty mariners and other men for the carriage of the king's artillery to France. July 28.

Nov. 8.

By K.

Commission to Thomas-Colage, king's serjeant at arms, to arrest and commit to the nearest gaol, until further order, Thomas William­ son, master of a balinger of the lord of Talbot, and others in the balinger who, as appears by a complaint to the king by John Dasse of Cologne, took a ship called le Grayer of Durdraght, of which Cornelius Brandson is master, laden at Durdraght with goods of the complainant and other merchants of the Hanse for London, while sailing to that city with the master and crew, and plundered the latter of the ship, goods and merchandise; and to seize the ship, goods and merchandise if these are extant, or their value if not extant, and restore them to the complainant and the said merchants.

Commission to Thomas Colege, king's serjeant at arms, to' arrest and take all persons hindering John Stevenes of London, merchant, from carrying out his licence to ship twenty thousand woolfells, called ' moreins' and 'shorlyng,' from Bishops Lenn to Holand and Seland, the king having learned that divers persons of Lynn propose to hinder him; and to bring any persons so arrested before the king in Chancery. Dogmersfield.

rules.rule: Corn may not be sold by show or sample. Dealers bring their laden carts and horses to the appointed markets, within Newgate before the Friars Minors and at Gracechurch, without unloading or storing anything on the way.
No corn to be sold before Prime is rung at St Paul’s.
Ships and boats bringing corn to Billingsgate, or anywhere on the Thames, stay on common sale for a whole day without selling in gross, so that ordinary people can buy what they need.
Corn, malt and salt coming by water must lie openly at Billingsgate or Queenhithe for three market days before any corn dealer may buy for resale.
Corn and malt from Cambridgeshire, Huntingdonshire, Bedfordshire and Ware go to the market at Gracechurch; from Barnet and the west, to Newgate.
Corn brought to Queenhithe by strangers is put on sale at Prime, in view of four reputable men chosen for the purpose.
There ought to be no corn-monger except at Queenhithe.
rules.src: Riley’s table of ordinances, from the Liber Horn

rules.rule: No corn sold at Billingsgate, Queenhithe or Gracechurch before the bells appointed for it have rung.
Riley’s glossary: the Pavement near St Michael le Quern, at the west end of Cheap, where a corn market was held.
Custom at Gracechurch: a foreign cart bringing corn or malt pays ½d.; a cart of cheese 2d.; two horses bringing corn or malt ¼d.
No fish, fresh or salt, to be put on stalls for sale anywhere but Bridge Street, Woolchurch and Old Fish Street.
Fresh-water fish to be brought to Bridge Street and Old Fish Street and sold there and nowhere else.
Birlsters, who carry fish about the streets, are not to stand in Cheap or elsewhere.
The fishmongers’ ordinance made under Gregory de Rokesley, mayor: two hallmotes a year, one held at the Bridge and the other at West (Old) Fish Street.

No fresh fish bought for resale before sunrise, nor salt fish before Prime. No forestalling within the bounds of the Chapel on the Bridge, Castle Baynard and Jordan’s Quay, and no buying from a vessel before her rope is ashore.
Strangers bringing lampreys of Nantes must sell them by the wall of St Margaret’s (New Fish Street); nobody may buy them for resale until the fourth day after they arrive.

rules.date: proclaimed the Friday before Pentecost, 18 Edward
rules.rule: Each basket of fish to hold one kind of fish, as good below as on top; offenders lose the fish and are held as cheats. To be cried at London Bridge and in Old Fish Street.
Boats bringing oysters, whelks, mussels or soles may stay on sale for one high tide and two ebbs; after that the shellfish are forfeit.
A cart bringing fish or poultry into Westcheap pays 2d.
Foreign poulterers stand by themselves and sell at the corner of Leadenhall; no denizen poulterer may stand there or deal with them.
Denizen poulterers stand beside the west wall of the church of St Michael on Cornhill, apart from the foreigners at Leadenhall.
Foreign poulterers who come in by Newgate and Aldersgate sell on the Pavement before the Friars Minors, near the fountain.
Denizen poulterers stand and sell before the church of St Nicholas at the Flesh Shambles, and do not deal with the foreigners.

Fixed prices: best goose 6d., capon 6d., hen 6d., rabbit with the skin 4d., pheasant 12d., heron 16d., twelve pigeons 8d. No foreign poulterer may lodge with a denizen poulterer or sell outside the open market.
Bakers bringing bread in carts may not sell to any regratress before they reach Cheap.
Bread, cheese, poultry, fruit, hides and skins, onions, garlic and other small victuals sold in Cheap and on Cornhill must stand midway between the kennels, so as not to block the street.
On fair days, pots, pans, hutches, coffers and other iron and brass ware may be sold only at Cornhill.
No market to be held on London Bridge, only in the places appointed elsewhere in the City.
No market in Cheap or on Cornhill after curfew is rung at St Paul’s.
No regrator of corn, fish or poultry may buy before Prime is rung at St Paul’s, or before the substantial men of the land and City have bought their provisions.
Carts of firewood, timber or charcoal may not stand in the City before their load is sold; they wait outside the gate, in Smithfield or another appointed place. Cornhill alone is excepted.
Custom of Woolchurch Haw, where a wool market was held: ½d. on wool sold to a foreigner, by the pound or the sack; ½d. on woolfells and on woollen yarn.
No one to sell hides except in the Seld of Friday Street.

No merchant, denizen or stranger, may go to the Pool or elsewhere on the Thames to meet wines or other goods, or board ships to buy, before the goods have come to land. Riley glosses the Pool as the river from the Tower to Limehouse.
Carters’ rates: merchandise from Wool Wharf to Cheap 4d.; water from Dowgate to Cheap 1½d.

ships: a second ship (master Eustace le Fevre)
ships.note: The City writes to Winchelsea: goods and papers of four Londoners, William de Merwell, John Vyncent, Thomas le Werreor and John Hurer, were seized from these ships by Winchelsea men who took them for French goods; the City certifies they belonged to London citizens.

ships: La Edmond de Loundres (master Martin Squirel)
ships.note: The City certifies to La Rochelle that the three ships, laden with Rochelle wine for John de Oxenford, Adam de Excestre and other vintners, reached the Pool and discharged their cargoes.

Winchelsea asks for salt taken from the ship of Robert son of John Alard, a baron of Winchelsea. London replies that every stranger, Cinque Ports men included, owed the Queen’s hithe 2d. on each sieve of five quarters.

ships: La Margarete of London (master John Thom)
ships.note: The City asks the king to help Stephen Aleyn recover goods shipped from Normandy: chased by Flemish pirates, the ship unloaded at Caux, where men of the abbot of Fécamp carried the goods off.

Writ for the mayor and sheriffs to question foreign and London merchants about the seizure of William Cauntepy’s ship by Reymund Spian of Bayonne and others, and the French king’s seizure of three English vessels in reprisal.
The City asks Boulogne to help Adam Hurel and John Genge recover their ship and its wool, seized on Good Friday during a truce by men of Boulogne, Calais and Wissant.
Inquest into a midnight assault on the mariners of the galleys in the parish of St Dunstan, Tower Ward; the jury named eleven attackers.

Writ to inquire into the complaint of Bernard del Compre of Prymerole that the king’s serjeant-at-arms seized 31 of his 50 casks of Bordeaux wine at London, alleging that Prymerole had gone over to the French king.
Thomas atte Wych and Thomas atte Leye loaded 82 quarters of corn for Sluys and undertook to bring back a certificate that it had been discharged there.
John de Pykenham and John de Graveneye pleaded guilty to forestalling malt they had bought at Billingsgate from the ship’s master, Robert Harriesone.
Robert de Appelby, the king’s serjeant-at-arms, certified that he had sold half the ship to Richard de Prestone of London.

ships: la Marye de Boloygne, renamed Notre Dame de Londres
ships.note: Thomas le Northerne, vintner, certified that he had sold the ship to Richard de Preston and John Maykyn and been paid.

Half the ship, arrested by the bailiff of Billingsgate at the suit of Adam Bury and John Tornegold as the property of the late Richard de Kayton, was delivered to Alice, wife of John de Horsford, when she proved her title.

ships: a ship freighted in Flanders (master John Outresson)
ships.note: Bartholomew Myne, Adam Lovekyn and other merchants sued their fellow freighters, Nicholas Sarduche, Guydo de Porte and others, over goods thrown overboard in a storm off Flanders before the ship reached Mardyck.

ships: le Seinte Marie Cog of Lübeck
ships.note: The attorney of Henry Feld of Lübeck acknowledged £70 14d. received from the servant of John Waryn of Lynn for freight of salt from the Bay to Bristol, and the indenture of freight was cancelled.

Certificate on the petition of Lodovicus Andree, merchant of Florence: the ship was freighted at Southampton with more than 500 sacks of wool for Pisa, with terms for the payment due to the count of Flanders if she carried more.

Certificate of a fraud: after the death of Nicholas Donat of Siena, pepperer of London, his attorney changed the marks on bales freighted at Sluys, so that goods consigned to Philip Nery of Florence appeared to be Donat’s and were arrested.

Terms of a sale: the buyer to send ships for the coal and the sellers to load within twelve working days, with an allowance of £320 for freight; also woad stored in a house of John Stodeye, and a ship at the Woodwharf sold for £60.

The City complains to Bruges that men of Sluys boarded a hakebot freighted by John Drewe, an apprentice, as she lay outside the piles at Sluys, drove off the crew and took ship and cargo, despite the guarantee of Bruges, Ypres and Ghent.

ships: Sconeweder of Sluys (master Henry Fitz Andrew)
ships.note: Writ to restore 46 millstones from Brie and a load of plaster, belonging to two burgesses of Sluys, seized at sea between Dover and Calais.

Peter Serdau of Genoa, arrested by Nicholas Exton, alderman of Billingsgate, as a suspected spy, was questioned by the mayor; witnesses swore he was an honest mariner who had come in a carrack to Southampton and meant to sail for Lombardy.
Dispute between Hugh Richardesson of Southampton, keeper of the balinger, and its owner John Bedon of Calais over its profits and expenses, settled by Richard de Preston and Richard Toky.
The master appoints Thomas Girdeler of London to collect freight money recovered from Ramon Monedeys, burgess of Bordeaux, in the sheriffs’ court.

ships: Seintemariebote (master William Prophet of West Lynn)
ships.note: The master sued William Jay of Swineshead, merchant, for freight of 30 weys of salt carried to London at 5s. a wey and unloaded unpaid.
Arbitration between John Burwell and Nicholas Horne, partners in the ship, over wine held at Middelburg and the cost of tackle, victuals and the wages of master and mariners.

ships: Seintmarie of Dartmouth (a barge owned by John Hawley)
ships.note: The master, Thomas Lynne, sued Genoese merchants (Octobone Grelo, Pelegrin Cataigne and their partners) who had chartered the barge at Seville.
Henry Sanday of Lucca, burgess of Venice, sold the ship and her gear to Gilbert Maghfeld, merchant of London, warranting her for a year and a day under the Law of Oléron.

ships: Sabater of Bayonne (master Perynanton de Blay)
ships.note: The master appointed Arnald William of Sedze and Henry Tylnay of London, vintner, his attorneys in English courts while abroad.

Inquest into insurgents who threatened him in Ivy Lane, parish of St Faith, until he bought his life for 60s.

c1381.who: Henry Plot of Cobham and others
c1381.text: Mainprises before John Northampton, mayor, of men held on suspicion of the insurrection but not indicted (Dec. 1381).

Sued John Lancastre of Hatfield Broad Oak, who on 14 June 1381 came with insurgents seeking him; Organ fled and buried cloth of gold, velvets, silks and linen worth £200 in the parish of St Olave Old Jewry, where they rotted.
Inquest on a complaint that he led rioters to the Savoy and St John’s; the jury found he went to St John’s, Clerkenwell, and stole a missal, bacon and bulls, but was not a leader.
Charged with saying that the city was badly governed and that John Constantyn, cordwainer, beheaded in Cheap for the rising of 11 February 1384, was wrongly condemned.
Bound over before Nicholas Brembre, mayor, with four mercers as sureties, to keep the peace and hold no gatherings.
The armourers and other misteries bring suspected men before Brembre, who are bailed to keep the peace.
Had said in Parliament that there would be no quiet in the city until an end was made of Nicholas Brembre; released on bail to six cordwainers.

By bill of p.s. etc.

Licence, for Nicholas Luke, merchant of Lombardy, to make exchanges with other merchants in the king's friendship beyond seas of merchandise or money to the value of 1,000 marks, provided that he does not take or send gold or silver out of the realm in coin or bullion. The like for Lewis de Portico, merchant of Lombardy. Feb. 5.

Corn, malt and salt coming by water must lie openly at Billingsgate or Queenhithe for three market days before a corn dealer may buy for resale.
The first vessel of the season from Yarmouth with white herrings owing full custom gives 200 herrings; every later one gives 100.

No custom on the carts of freemen carrying wool landed at Queenhithe.

trades.name: Gascon wine
trades.basis: Vintage fleet in late autumn and the "reek" fleet in spring (M. K. James, Studies in the Medieval Wine Trade). Wine was landed in the Vintry; whether large ships still passed the drawbridge in the fifteenth century needs checking.

other: Sailors’ wages London to Bordeaux and La Rochelle differ “in vintage time” and “in time of reek”: the two wine voyages of the year.
Black Book I, p. 139
Billingsgate took 2d. a tun on wine owing custom; the sheriff took 2d. a tun on wine coming into the City.
Munimenta III, pp. 62, 72
ev.finding: Two wine voyages a year are attested (vintage and reek). The months are not.

trades.name: Wool to Flanders
trades.basis: Wool customed at Wool Wharf and shipped in spring and autumn fleets; staple sites moved several times before 1363 (Lloyd, The English Wool Trade). From 1353 the staple was held in England, Westminster among the staple towns (LB G, p. 16; CPR 1350–54, p. 511).

other: Statute of the Staple, 27 Edward III, appointing staple towns in England, Wales and Ireland; John Wrothe is mayor of the staple at Westminster.
LB G, p. 16
Carpenters taken to build houses in Westminster palace for the wool staple to be held there, and a new landing-stage towards the Thames for wool brought to it.
Roger Roter acts as mayor of the staple of Westminster.
ev.finding: Correction: from 1353 the staple was at Westminster, not overseas. The model still sends wool to Flanders for 1353–62.

trades.name: Wool to the Calais staple
trades.basis: Staple fixed at Calais from 1363 (with interruptions); fleets often sailed in convoy.

ev.finding: The 1418 wool ships left the Thames for Southampton to join the king’s expedition, not for Calais.

trades.name: Cloth to the Brabant marts
trades.basis: Mercers and Merchant Adventurers shipping for the four marts of Antwerp and Bergen-op-Zoom (Easter, Whitsun, St Bavo, Cold). Timings to be checked (Sutton, The Mercery of London).

ev.finding: No entry in these extracts ties London cloth shipments to the Brabant marts.

trades.name: Hanse cogs (Baltic)
trades.basis: Baltic navigation largely closed in winter; Hanse merchants landed at the Steelyard (Lloyd, England and the German Hanse).

other: Hanse merchants Hermann Vynthorp and Aubrey Clippyng shipped copper, wax, grey fur and iron in the Dordrecht cog wrecked at Reculver; a barrel of peltry of John Swart, Hanse merchant, was cast ashore and concealed.

trades.name: Stockfish (Bergen)
trades.basis: Norwegian stockfish via Bergen, a Hanse-dominated trade, chiefly in summer.

other: Stockfish from Prussia paid ¼d. a hundred at Billingsgate.
Munimenta III, p. 72

trades.name: Iceland voyages
trades.basis: English voyages to Iceland from the 1410s, mainly from East Anglia and Bristol; London’s share needs checking.

other: Le Jacob of Hamburg, laden in Iceland with 26,000 stockfish of Lübeck and Hamburg merchants “to take to the port of London”, was driven ashore near Hartlepool and plundered (after this period).

trades.name: Yarmouth herring
trades.basis: Yarmouth herring fair, Michaelmas to Martinmas.

other: The first vessel of the season from Yarmouth with white herrings gave 200 herrings at Billingsgate, later ones 100.
Munimenta III, p. 71
London to Scania: three mariners shared the portage of a last of herrings.
Black Book I, pp. 140–41

trades.name: Sea-coal (Newcastle)
trades.basis: Coastal colliers, mostly in the sailing season.

other: London to Newcastle: a mariner’s wage 4s. and two quarters of coal free of charge.
Black Book I, p. 141
Sea-coal paid ¼d. for two quarters at Billingsgate.
Munimenta III, p. 71

trades.name: Italian galleys
trades.basis: Venetian Flanders galleys and Genoese carracks called mainly at Southampton; London calls (Galley Quay) need checking for frequency.

ev.finding: Correction: galleys were in the Pool by 1337, when their crews were attacked in St Dunstan’s parish (CPMR i, p. 146), so the model’s start date of 1400 is too late. Genoese carracks used Southampton (1372, 1382), and in 1452 Genoese wines came from Sandwich to London in a great boat.

trades.name: Iberian trade
trades.basis: Castilian and Portuguese shipping (Childs, Anglo-Castilian Trade).

other: London to Lisbon: a mariner’s wage 20s. and the portage of a tun.
Black Book I, p. 139

trades.name: Low Countries goods
trades.basis: Year-round short-sea traffic; cf. the Dordrecht cog of 1389.

trades.name: Coastal corn
trades.basis: East Anglian and Kentish grain to Queenhithe and Billingsgate, peaking after harvest.

other: Corn, malt and salt coming by water had to lie openly at Billingsgate or Queenhithe for three market days before corn dealers could buy for resale.
Munimenta III, p. 182
ev.finding: The 1347 licences ship wheat out of London to Bordeaux, and in 1344 Londoners loaded corn for Sluys (CPMR i, p. 160); the model has no outbound grain.
